newsitem.title: BOSNIA: US peacekeepers start pullout from peaceful Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: US peacekeepers start pullout from peaceful Bosnia.

text.p: U.S. troops have begun to pull out of Bosnia after a 12-month peacekeeping tour, leaving behind a calm but politically still unstable country and questions over how to keep they peace once they have gone.

"Three units left their bases in Tuzla area on Thursday, the 17th Signal Brigade, 4-29 Field Artillery Brigade and the fire support team, 152 people in all," U.S. spokesman in Slavonski Brod, Captain Steve Metz told Reuters.
"A hundred more people are scheduled to leave tomorrow."
They are part of the 15,000-strong U.S. force serving in Bosnia in the NATO-led peace implementation force (IFOR).

Their departure, which started on Wednesday, is the start of a large-scale withdrawal of American troops in line with U.S. President Bill Clinton's promise to pull them out by the end of IFOR's mandate on December 20.
Some 60,000 international peacekeepers arrived in Bosnia after the warring parties struck a peace accord in Dayton Ohio, last November, ending 3-1/2 years of war.
The Pentagon has now dispatched a 5,000-strong, more mobile "covering force" to provide security for the pullout.
The first contingent of that force left Germany for Bosnia on Tuesday and some of those may stay on until next March.

But the international peace coordinator for Bosnia, Carl Bildt, said on Thursday foreign contingents of troops should remain in Bosnia in 1997 and 1998 if the country is to stand any chance of recovering from the recent war.
NATO is pushing for a follow-on force with a U.S. presence to remain in Bosnia after December.

"The mission of this military presence would primarily be deterrent, to provide reassurance that there are no military options and no military threat, thus providing the conditions necessary for political reconciliation, re-integration and reconstruction," he said in a speech in London.
His words highlighted divisions plaguing the country after Serbs failed to join governing bodies elected on September 14.
But Colum Murphy, spokesman for Bildt, said the Serb member of Bosnia's three-man presidency was showing signs of reversing his opposition to the body.
Momcilo Krajisnik failed to attend the presidency's inaugural session last weekend, infuriating the international community.
Other tensions remain although Bosnian Serb police were showing restraint in three northeast Bosnian villages under their control recently resettled by former Moslem residents.
The Serbs joined IFOR and international police (IPTF) in joint patrols to reassert authority over the district.
IPTF spokesman Alex Ivanko confirmed earlier reports that the Serb police had found a small arms cache in one village and faced angry protests when they tried to arrest a house owner.
IFOR and IPTF were able to defuse the situation, Ivanko said, and were continuing random searches of houses for possible weapons, but without the Serb police.
Bosnia faces further problems as it tries to asorb thousands of refugees the local German state authorities want to deport to rid themselves of a costly burden.

U.N. refugee agencies say it is premature to return displaced people to largely unreconstructed Bosnia where large areas are already overcrowded with people, houses are destroyed and a harsh winter is about to set in.

Bavaria deported the first of some 320,000 Bosnian war refugees from Germany on Wednesday and Bonn took another step on Thursday, signing a repatriation agreement with Belgrade to send home some 135,000 refugees to Yugoslavia from December.
